headline: Indonesia and the EU sign a big trade deal

chunks.text: On November 21, 2026, the European Union, a group of countries in Europe, signed a [[trade deal]] with Indonesia in Belgium, home of the EU's [[main offices]]. A trade deal makes buying and selling between countries easier. They also signed a second agreement to protect [[investors]]. The talks {{dragged on}} for about a decade. EU governments {{signed off on}} the deal on November 18. Indonesia is Southeast Asia's [[largest economy]].

verbs.why: Some meetings drag on until late at night. A bad cold sometimes drags on for weeks. The trade talks between the EU and Indonesia dragged on for about a decade.

verbs.wrong: To sell goods at a market
verbs.why: The manager signs off on every new hire. Parents sign off on school trips before children can go. EU governments signed off on the trade deal on November 18, 2026.

chunks.text: The deal will {{do away with}} [[tariffs]], or taxes on goods from other countries, on over 98 percent of European goods sold to Indonesia, the EU says. Indonesia's 50 percent tariff on European cars will end within five years. [[In return]], the EU will drop tariffs [[right away]] on about 90 percent of the types of Indonesian goods. It will {{phase out}} tariffs on most other goods over 3 to 15 years.

verbs.why: Many restaurants do away with paper menus and use phones instead. Some schools do away with homework for young children. The deal will do away with tariffs on over 98 percent of European goods sold to Indonesia.

verbs.correct: To remove something slowly, in steps
verbs.wrong: To check goods at the border
verbs.why: Car makers phase out old models over a few years. Some stores phase out plastic bags over many months. The EU will phase out most of its other tariffs on Indonesian goods over 3 to 15 years.

chunks.text: Indonesia expects its sales to the EU to {{go up}} by about 14 percent. [[Clothing]], shoes and [[vegetable oils]] should gain the most. Worries about palm oil and [[deforestation]], the clearing of forests, {{held up}} the talks. The deal has a [[special section]] on palm oil to help {{iron out}} these problems. Both sides also hoped to reduce [[harm]] from U.S. tariffs. The EU wants to {{branch out}} and trade with more [[parts of the world]].

verbs.why: Rent goes up in many cities every year. Ticket prices go up during the summer. Indonesia expects its sales to the EU to go up by about 14 percent.
Heavy snow often holds up flights in winter. A missing form sometimes holds up a bank loan. Worries about palm oil and the clearing of forests held up the trade talks.
Business partners iron out problems before they sign a contract. A good manager irons out problems between team members. The deal has a special section on palm oil to help iron out these problems.
Many bakeries branch out and sell coffee too. Some farmers branch out into new crops when prices fall. The EU wants to branch out and trade with more parts of the world.

chunks.text: The deal still had to {{go through}} the European Parliament, where EU [[lawmakers]] vote. Indonesia also had to [[ratify]] it, or give it final approval. Officials hoped it could {{kick in}} early in 2027. Lower EU tariffs on Indonesian goods under an older program were set to {{run out}} on January 1, 2027. Indonesia's economy minister called the signing a [[milestone]], not an [[end goal]]. The EU said the deal would {{pay off}}, making both economies billions of euros larger by 2042.

verbs.wrong: To be weighed on a scale
verbs.why: Some house sales never go through. A big bank loan often takes weeks to go through. The trade deal still had to go through the European Parliament.

verbs.correct: To start to have an effect
verbs.why: The medicine kicks in after about twenty minutes. New tax rules usually kick in on January 1. Officials hoped the trade deal could kick in early in 2027.

verbs.correct: To end after a set time
verbs.why: Our lease runs out at the end of the month. Many free trials run out after one month. Lower EU tariffs on Indonesian goods under an older program were set to run out on January 1, 2027.

verbs.wrong: To be kept in a warehouse
verbs.why: Hard work at school often pays off later in life. A good ad usually pays off with more customers. The EU said the trade deal would pay off, making both economies billions of euros larger by 2042.

mainIdea.s: The European Union and Indonesia signed a deal that will end most taxes on goods traded between them. Indonesia hopes to sell more to Europe, but lawmakers still had to approve it.
mainIdea.why: The deal will do away with tariffs on almost all goods. It still had to go through the European Parliament, and Indonesia had to ratify it.

mainIdea.s: Indonesia agreed to drop its tariffs on European products, while Europe keeps its own taxes on Indonesian goods. The new rules for both sides start right away, with no further votes.
mainIdea.why: Close, but both sides will do away with tariffs. The deal can only kick in after the European Parliament and Indonesia approve it.

mainIdea.s: Indonesia stopped selling palm oil to other countries for three months to keep cooking oil cheap at home. Farmers protested the ban outside government buildings in several cities.
mainIdea.why: This story is about a trade deal between the EU and Indonesia. The two sides signed it after talks dragged on for about a decade.

tf.s: The EU and Indonesia signed a trade deal after talks dragged on for years.
tf.why: They signed the deal on November 21, 2026, after about a decade of talks.

tf.s: The deal will do away with tariffs on only a few kinds of goods.
tf.why: It will end tariffs on over 98 percent of European goods sold to Indonesia, and on most Indonesian goods too.

tf.s: Indonesia expects its sales to the EU to fall because of the deal.
tf.why: Indonesia expects its sales to the EU to go up by about 14 percent.

tf.s: Worries about palm oil and forests held up the trade talks.
tf.why: Fears about palm oil and the clearing of forests slowed the talks, so the deal has a special section to iron out these problems.

tf.s: The EU wants to branch out and trade with more parts of the world.
tf.why: Both sides also hoped the deal would reduce the harm from U.S. tariffs, so the EU wants more trade partners.

tf.s: The trade deal started on the same day that it was signed.
tf.why: It still had to go through the European Parliament, and officials hoped it could kick in early in 2027.

lines.text: Did you hear that the EU and Indonesia signed a trade deal?
I did. Didn't those talks {{drag on}} for years?
For about a decade. They finally [[sealed the deal]] in Belgium on November 21.
[[Slowly but surely]]. So what actually changes?
Both sides will {{do away with}} most tariffs. Those are taxes on goods from other countries.
No. The EU will {{phase out}} some tariffs slowly, over three to fifteen years.
It expects its sales to Europe to {{go up}} by about 14 percent. Clothing and shoes should gain the most.
I heard palm oil was a problem, though.
It was. Worries about forests {{held up}} the talks, so the deal has a special section to {{iron out}} those problems.
And why does Europe want this deal?
The EU wants to {{branch out}} and trade more with other parts of the world. Both sides also want less harm from U.S. tariffs.
So does it start right away?
Not yet. It still has to {{go through}} the European Parliament, and Indonesia has to ratify it.
So they still need to [[cross the finish line]].
Right. Officials said they hoped it could {{kick in}} early in 2027. Lower EU tariffs on Indonesian goods under an older program were set to {{run out}} on January 1.
If it {{pays off}}, lower tariffs could [[make a big difference]] for small businesses there.
